# uia-tree

Turn a Windows GUI into a JSON tree with screen coordinates.

```ts
import { uia } from 'uia-tree';

const snap = await uia.readForeground();

const save = snap.find({ role: 'Button', name: 'Save' });
if (save) console.log('click at', save.click);   // { x: 1778, y: 390 }
```

Reads the Windows **UI Automation** tree — the accessibility layer screen
readers use. Unlike image matching, nothing has to be captured in advance: you
ask what is on screen and get an answer, with exact pixel coordinates.

Windows x64 only. The compiled binary ships with the package.

## Why this exists

Image matching answers *"is this picture present?"* — which needs you to know
what to look for. This answers *"what is on screen?"*, which is what you need
when you don't know in advance. That makes it useful for

- **scraping** — links with their hrefs, inputs with their values, all the text
- **automation** — find a button by name, click its coordinates
- **recording** — turn a click coordinate back into *what was there*
- **agents** — hand a model a list of named, numbered, clickable things

It pairs with an input library (such as `augui`): `uia-tree` tells you *where*,
the other one *does* it.

## Reading a window

```ts
await uia.listWindows();                    // what's open
await uia.readForeground();                 // the focused window
await uia.readByTitle('Chrome');            // first match, or null
await uia.readWindow(handle);               // by handle from listWindows

await uia.elementAt(x, y);                  // just the element under a point
await uia.focusedElement();                 // what has keyboard focus
```

Options:

```ts
await uia.readForeground({
  includeAll: false,    // keep layout containers too (default false)
  maxDepth: 50,
  maxElements: 5000,    // guard against huge trees
  region: { x: 0, y: 0, width: 800, height: 600 },   // only this area
  retries: 3,           // for Chromium's lazy tree — see below
});
```

## What you get

```ts
const snap = await uia.readForeground();

snap.window        // "Nasos-NL-811.conf - Notepad"
snap.framework     // "Win32"
snap.tookMs        // 45
snap.elements      // flat, depth-first; elements[0] is the window
```

Each element:

```ts
{
  id: 17,                      // index in this snapshot — not an identity
  depth: 4,
  role: 'MenuItem',            // Button, Edit, Hyperlink, Text, ...
  name: 'File',                // the visible label
  value: undefined,            // input contents; for a link, its href
  automationId: '',            // dev-assigned id — the best thing to match on
  className: '',
  rect:  { x: 1619, y: 406, width: 41, height: 32 },
  click: { x: 1639, y: 422 },  // centre of rect, ready for a mouse move
  framework: 'XAML',
  enabled: true,
  offscreen: false,            // scrolled out of view — NOT hidden
  focusable: true,
  parent: 16,
  children: [],
}
```

### Finding things

```ts
snap.find({ role: 'Button', name: 'Save' });
snap.find({ nameContains: 'Save' });
snap.find({ automationId: 'submitBtn' });     // most stable where available
snap.findAll({ role: 'MenuItem' });
snap.findOrThrow({ role: 'Edit' });           // throws instead of returning null
```

### Ready-made views

```ts
snap.interactive   // everything clickable/typeable, enabled and on screen
snap.links         // name = link text, value = href
snap.inputs        // Edit and ComboBox, value = contents
snap.text          // all visible text, in reading order

snap.childrenOf(el);
snap.parentOf(el);
snap.pathTo(el);   // root -> ... -> el

snap.toText();     // indented table — fastest way to see what you got
snap.toTree();     // nested object, if you want the shape
```

## Scraping, for real

On Hacker News in a normal Chrome window:

```
517 elements in 39ms — 229 links

"Mold Linker Version 3.0.0 Release – Rewritten in Rust"
    -> https://github.com/rui314/mold/releases/tag/v3.0.0
"roflcopter69"  -> https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=roflcopter69
"333 comments"  -> https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49917536

INPUTS
  Address and search bar = "news.ycombinator.com"
```

Titles, authors, comment counts, timestamps — each with its href **and** its
click coordinate. Not the DOM, but for many jobs it is enough, and it comes
from the user's own browser with their own session.

```ts
const snap = await uia.readByTitle('Hacker News');
const stories = snap!.links.filter((l) => l.name.length > 15 && l.value?.startsWith('http'));
for (const s of stories) console.log(s.name, '->', s.value);
```

## Speed — and why

| window | elements | time |
|---|---|---|
| Notepad | 37 | 45 ms |
| Chrome (Hacker News) | 517 | 39 ms |
| VS Code (warm) | ~3000 | ~230 ms |

That speed comes from one thing. Reading UIA properties one at a time costs
**one cross-process COM call each** — 3000 elements × 10 properties would be
30,000 round trips and take seconds. This package bulk-fetches the whole
subtree in a single call (`CacheRequest`), then reads every field in-process.

Fast enough to call per step in a loop.

## Chromium needs its accessibility tree woken up

Chrome, Edge and Electron build their accessibility tree **only when something
asks**, and the first read often returns a stub. This is the one real gotcha.

**Electron wakes up on its own, progressively.** Three consecutive reads of VS
Code returned **6 → 241 → 3011** elements. The `retries` option handles this.

**Chrome page content is less willing.** Without help you get only the browser
chrome — Back, Reload, the address bar — and a `Document` node with no
children. The reliable fix is to launch it with

```
chrome.exe --force-renderer-accessibility
```

which costs some CPU for the session, and is exactly why it is off by default.

**So: a small tree means "not ready yet", not "nothing there."** Read twice
before concluding a window is empty.

## Gotchas

- **`id` is per-snapshot.** It is an array index, not an identity. Re-reading
  renumbers everything. Match on `automationId`, or role + name.
- **Coordinates are absolute screen pixels**, valid only while the window stays
  put. Move or resize it and they all change — so read fresh rather than
  caching positions.
- **Physical pixels.** On a DPI-scaled display, a process that is not
  DPI-aware will read coordinates in a different space than it clicks in.
  Worth testing if your machines use scaling.
- **`value` is often empty** where an app does not implement `ValuePattern`.
- **Custom-drawn Win32** can collapse to a single opaque `Pane` — UIA cannot
  see inside an app that paints its own widgets.
- **Text has no per-line coordinates.** A text editor gives you one `Document`
  with the whole contents in `value`. Per-character geometry needs the UIA
  TextPattern API, which this does not expose.
- **A locked session renders nothing**, but UIA reads over COM rather than from
  the screen, so it is far less affected than screen capture. Test it directly
  if unattended runs matter to you.

## Playground

In a clone of the source (not part of the npm package):

```sh
npm run dump                   # the foreground window, as a table
npm run dump -- --list         # what windows are open
npm run dump -- Chrome         # by title
npm run dump -- Chrome --json  # JSON
npm run dump -- Chrome --all   # include layout containers
npm run watch-clicks           # name whatever is under the cursor
```

`watch-clicks` is the germ of a recorder: the hard part of "replay what I did"
is turning a coordinate back into a durable description of what was there, and
`elementAt` does that.

## Build from source

Needs a Rust toolchain with the `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` target.

```sh
npm install
npm run build          # release + TypeScript
npm run build:debug    # faster, for iterating
```

## Changelog

### 0.1.1

- **`inputs` and `interactive` now include `Document`.** Some apps expose their
  main text area as a `Document` rather than an `Edit` — Windows 11 Notepad has
  no `Edit` anywhere, only `Document "Text editor"`. Both helpers previously
  omitted it, so the only typeable thing in the window was invisible to them
  with nothing to signal it was missing.
- **`inputs` is now sorted largest first** and excludes disabled/offscreen
  elements. In an editor the main content area is almost always what you mean.
